name: Science as technique and the 'power philosophy'
plain_explanation: Beyond science as a body of theory, there is 'practical science' -- technology -- which gives human beings, collectively rather than individually, immense power over nature. Because this power is ethically neutral (it says what can be done, not what should be done), and because it requires large-scale organization, it tends to produce philosophies obsessed with skillful process and control rather than with worthwhile ends.
precise_definition: Russell's account of practical science ('an attempt to change the world') as socially rather than individually empowering, requiring 'the co-operation of a large number of individuals organized under a single direction,' and as ethically neutral, giving rise to 'power philosophies' that 'tend to regard everything non-human as mere raw material' and value only 'the skilfulness of the process,' not ends -- which Russell calls 'the most dangerous form' of madness in his own day.
why_it_mattered: This is Russell's second diagnosed 'form of madness,' complementing the anarchistic extreme of subjectivism, and he explicitly states that 'a sane philosophy should provide an antidote' to it -- framing the normative stakes of the entire book.
historical_origin: Traced to the practical use of science in warfare from Galileo and Leonardo onward, later extended to machine production and the use of steam and electricity.
examples: Galileo and Leonardo obtaining government employment through claims to improve artillery and fortification
The growth of machine production and the use of steam, then electricity
influence_on_later_thinkers: Implicitly frames Russell's critical stance toward twentieth-century totalitarian 'power philosophies,' discussed later in the book.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly political: control of the 'vast organizations' that scientific technique requires determines what purposes power is put to.
